newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries jittery in thin London trade, eye FOMC.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries jittery in thin London trade, eye FOMC.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were broadly steady in light volume in London on Tuesday with all eyes focused on the first leg of a two-day Federal Open Market Committee Meeting (FOMC), analysts said.

"The market is a bundle of nerves and mixed emotions ahead of the FOMC," said David Bloom, international economist at HSBC James Capel. "But the FOMC is just talking shop today and we get the big news on Wednesday."
Traders said the FOMC would overshadow key economic indicators including the June report from the National Association of Purchasing Management and May leading indicators.

"I think the NAPM is not too relevant in the context," said Nick Benton, U.S. Treasury salesman at BankAmerica in London. "Everyone's waiting for the FOMC and payrolls. I don't see the market doing much ahead of those two."
The FOMC meeting was expected to start at 1300 GMT.
By 0925 GMT, the benchmark long bond was quoted at 97-28, yielding 6.792, unchanged from Tokyo levels and 2/32 below New York's close.
September T-bond futures were unchanged from the Chicago settlement at 111-02 in automated trade.
Treasuries edged lower in New York overnight after strong housing sales and a robust Chicago purchasing managers report put pressure on the market.
Both Benton and Bloom said they thought all market players would have their positions set ahead of the FOMC.
"The market has factored in no rate rise, but I don't think anyone would be completely surprised to see the Fed raise interest rates," Bloom said.
All 36 economists in a Reuters poll on Monday were unanimous in predicting no change in interest rates at the FOMC meeting.

The June NAPM, due at 1400 GMT, would show a reading of 56.4, down from the 57.1 the previous month, according to a Reuters survey. A reading above 50.0 indicates an expanding manufacturing economy, according to the NAPM.
The poll forecast Thursday's June payrolls to rise sharply to 222,000, up from 138,000 the previous month.
